definition: Fairness in machine learning (ML) refers to the various attempts to correct algorithmic bias in automated decision processes based on ML models.
details: Decisions made by such models after a learning process may be considered unfair if they were based on variables considered sensitive (e.g., gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or disability). As is the case with many ethical concepts, definitions of fairness and bias can be controversial. In general, fairness and bias are considered relevant when the decision process impacts people's lives. Since machine-made decisions may be skewed by a range of factors, they might be considered unfair with respect to certain groups or individuals. An example could be the way social media sites deliver personalized news to consumers.

explainer.lead: Fairness in machine learning is about noticing and trying to correct bias in decisions made by learned models. It matters when those decisions affect people’s lives, because a model may treat groups or individuals unfairly even when the process is automated.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot choosing which stories to show each person, but its choices are skewed because of things like someone’s gender or ethnicity. Fairness means checking whether its choices are unjust and trying to fix that. People can disagree about exactly what counts as fair, just as they can disagree about fair rules for a game.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, fairness work examines whether a model’s decisions are skewed with respect to sensitive variables, particular groups, or individuals. It is especially relevant when automated decisions affect people’s lives, and it involves attempts to correct the resulting algorithmic bias. A central pitfall is treating fairness as a single settled definition: both fairness and bias can be controversial, and decisions may be skewed by a range of factors.
tiers.paperLevel: A general formulation considers a learned decision Yhat, sensitive attributes A such as gender or ethnicity, and the effects of that decision on groups or individuals. Fairness work asks whether Yhat is unfairly skewed with respect to A or other factors and seeks to correct that algorithmic bias. There is no universally accepted definition of fairness or bias, so the appropriate criterion can remain contested.

explainer.example: A social media site uses a learned model to deliver personalized news. If the delivery process is skewed by ethnicity or another sensitive variable, some groups may be treated unfairly; fairness work would examine that skew and attempt to correct it.

explainer.intuition: A model can automate a decision without making that decision just. Fairness asks whether the learned process disadvantages people unfairly and how that bias might be corrected.
howItWorks: Consider a decision produced by a model after learning.
Examine whether sensitive variables or other factors have skewed it.
Assess possible unfairness toward groups or individuals.
Attempt to correct the identified algorithmic bias.
explainer.whyItMatters: Machine-made decisions can affect people’s lives while still carrying bias from a range of factors. Fairness makes those effects open to scrutiny rather than assuming that automation guarantees equal or just treatment.
misconceptions: Fairness has one universally agreed definition.
Only sensitive variables can skew a model’s decisions.
An automated decision is fair simply because a model made it.
